Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU - Google Developers Blog 

# Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

OCT. 20, 2026

 Qi Zhou Principal Software Engineer 

 Chris Chan Group Product Manager 

As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).

## Background

For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. vLLM and SGLang already run on TPU through JAX-based backend, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.

So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.

Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.

...

### Workload support

Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.

Here’s the list of supported features:

- Agentic & Multi-Turn: Automatic prefix caching, including for hybrid models; KV cache offloading to host memory and Managed Lustre through TPU Sync; tool calling and structured output
- Interactive & Low Latency: Speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark and n-gram drafters
- High-throughput Batch: Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism
- Long Context: Context parallelism for prefill and decode; FP8 KV cache; host KV offloading
- Disaggregated Serving: Prefill and decode on separate hosts over TPU Sync, including between different parallel layouts
- Multimodal: Vision-language models with image and video input; embedding models
- Very Large Models: Hybrid and sparse-attention architectures, tensor, data, expert, pipeline and context parallelism across hosts; FP8, FP4 (MXFP4, NVFP4), INT8 and INT4 checkpoints

...

## Running today in production & public benchmarks

Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.

Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.

...

## Getting started

Get started today:

- vLLM-TorchTPU: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu
- SGLang-TorchTPU: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu
- TorchTPU: https://github.com/google-pytorch/torch_tpu

signals.title: Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog

# Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference

October 21, 2026 19 min read

Table of Contents

Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features:

- Broad device support: Supports NVIDIA GPU architectures from Turing onward, along with CUDA-compatible devices such as T-Head's Zhenwu 810E.
- Extensive quantization support: A unified architecture supports diverse combinations of weight and activation formats for dense and MoE workloads, covering a wide range of integer and floating-point types, bit widths, and scaling schemes.
- Strong execution performance: Significantly outperforms existing implementations from vLLM Marlin, FlashInfer, and DeepGEMM across many representative workloads.

Repository: github.com/vllm-project/humming

...

Background

As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency.

Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space.

These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low.

...

## General-Purpose Architecture

Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components.

...

### Broad Device Support

Humming's unified architecture enables broad GPU support. For NVIDIA GPUs, Humming fully supports every architecture from Turing onward, bringing a common quantized computing framework to multiple generations of hardware.

The unified JIT architecture also makes it straightforward to extend Humming to other GPUs compatible with CUDA programming. Humming already fully supports T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, bringing its shared kernels and tuning capabilities to more hardware platforms.

...

#### End-to-End Inference Performance

Humming's W4A8 gains extend to model serving. In our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash test on eight H20 GPUs with TP=8, keeping the model's MXFP4 weights unchanged and switching MoE execution from Marlin W4A16 (BF16 activations) to Humming W4A8 (tokenwise FP8 activations) improves end-to-end throughput by approximately 14%–43% and reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by approximately 25%–32%. The throughput advantage grows with concurrency: at concurrency 64, output throughput rises from 442.37 to 633.94 tokens/s, while mean time per output token (TPOT) falls by approximately 31%.

signals.title: llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference | Google Cloud Blog

October 20, 2026

##### Mark Lohmeyer

Product Manager

##### Nov 4: Agentic Data Cloud Event

Today at the PyTorch Conference, we released llm-d 1.0, an open-source, Kubernetes-native stack for distributed LLM inference. Co-founded by Google with Red Hat, IBM and others, we worked with a community of more than 500 contributors over 25 organizations on this Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, bringing together two important communities: PyTorch, where vLLM and SGLang serve models, and Kubernetes, where distributed systems run and scale in production.

...

llm-d solves this for teams serving their own models by turning a cluster of model servers into a coordinated serving pool. During the PyTorch Conference keynote, we showed this in action with 1,000 sandboxed agents on Agent Substrate on GKE hitting a single llm-d endpoint across vLLM, SGLang, and a mixed fleet of Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. As traffic scaled across the three stages below, cache-aware routing and tiered KV cache kept each agent's steps on the replicas holding its context, while flow control queued bursty agent loops so interactive requests stayed fast.

...

### What 1.0 provides

llm-d already delivered prefix- and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch inference across Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. These capabilities provide:

- Multi-tenant quality of service. Priority and fairness-aware routing via llm-d flow control, helping latency-sensitive requests and bursty agent workloads share a fleet to meet SLOs without starving one another.
- A stable foundation. v1 APIs and a hardened request path, validated on multiple clouds and accelerator types.
- Safer upgrades. Router high availability and zero-downtime updates, alongside DisaggregatedSet, which orchestrates prefill/decode-aware rolling updates without dropping context or disrupting active sessions.
- Agent-aware serving. Session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, and native Responses API state, helping agents reuse context across turns.
- Expanded TPU integration. Native PyTorch model serving with TorchTPU co-operative time-slicing to raise throughput and utilization across Google Cloud TPU fleets.

The components are designed so that you can compose them into your own bespoke production environment. Keep your engine, model and cluster, and adopt only the serving components and configurations you need.

...

On an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), prefix-aware routing plus host memory offload cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by more than 85% and raised total throughput 2.4x versus a plain Kubernetes Service, as of October 2026 (source).

...

During RL training, accelerators often sit idle 40% to 60% of the time during rollout generation or weight updates. llm-d now supports Google Cloud TPU and GPU time-slicing to interleave async inference into those quiet cycles, raising aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a ~40% baseline to >70% (source).

Benchmarks you can trust

Tuning a distributed inference stack across routers, KV cache tiers, and prefill/decode pools takes repeatable measurement under realistic multi-turn load. Prism is llm-d’s open-source analysis dashboard for exploring published benchmarks across llm-d’s well-lit paths, backed by standardized llm-d-benchmark recipes and inference-perf workloads. Inspect the exact configurations behind the numbers, or upload runs from your own cluster to compare throughput, latency, and cost curves side by side.

...

### In production

This GKE llm-d stack carries production traffic, and it has been tested at fleet scale:

- Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI) serves production traffic through GKE Inference Gateway, doubling its prefix cache hit rate from 35% to 70%, cutting TTFT by more than 35% for coding agents and cutting P95 TTFT by more than 50% under bursty chat traffic (source).
- In a published benchmark across a 17,000-node multi-region GKE deployment serving a mixture-of-experts model in the US and Europe, multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway and the llm-d router scaled throughput 2.9x across three clusters with a 99.9% success rate and less than 1% routing overhead (source).
- In a published benchmark on A3 Mega cluster serving a 70B-parameter model, llm-d with multi-connector KV cache offloading to Google Cloud Managed Lustre in addition to Host CPU RAM, delivered an approximately 40% improvement in TTFT and a 30% reduction in end-to-end latency responding to 50k-token prompts compared to CPU RAM offload only, while reducing GPU-hour requirements by nearly 60% (source).

signals.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed, Rerank, and Parse: Advancing Agents with World-Class Retrieval Models
signals.excerpt:
# NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed, Rerank, and Parse: Advancing Agents with World-Class Retrieval Models

Author: Yauhen Babakhin, Ryan Chesler, Jiarui Cai, Sean Sodha, Isabel Hulseman
Published: 2026-10-21T10:41:36Z
Source: huggingface.co
Language: en

## Story

# NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed, Rerank, and Parse: Advancing Agents with World-Class Retrieval Models
Published October 21, 2026
Yauhen Babakhin
Isabel Hulseman
ihulseman0220
An agent’s answers depend on the evidence it can retrieve. When that evidence is incomplete or irrelevant, the agent will repeat searches and inspect additional documents, consuming more inference tokens before completing the task. Better retrieval can help agents reach grounded answers with fewer wasted tokens. At enterprise scale, that waste leads to massive inefficiencies. Agents need the right retrieval models and systems to reach insights faster.
Today, we are expanding the **Nemotron Retriever** collection with new open, commercially available models for embedding, reranking, and document extraction. The new models include Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B BF16, 1B BF16, 1B NVFP4, Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B BF16, and Nemotron 3.5 Parse at 631M parameters.
Together, these state-of-the-art models bring multimodal retrieval, relevance ranking, and document processing to enterprise agent workflows.
#### Better Retrieval for More Efficient Agents
Retrieval quality affects both the answers an agent produces and the LLM inference cost. Relevant evidence can help the agent answer a question or better decide its next step, and reranking improves the quality of evidence that enters its context.
Consider an agent asked to identify products at risk of stockouts next quarter and explain why. It must combine demand forecasts in charts, inventory levels in tables, and supplier lead times in reports, then reason about whether replenishment will arrive before inventory runs out. Completing the task requires finding the relevant evidence across documents and using it together in the analysis.
To understand how retrieval affects the agent’s ability to combine evidence and complete a task, we evaluated Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank across ViDoRe v3, BRIGHT, and BrowseComp-Plus. ViDoRe v3 uses combined text and image inputs, while BRIGHT and BrowseComp-Plus use text-only inputs. In this pipeline, an agent queries the corpus using a search tool, inspects the evidence, and refines its next search attempt to find the most relevant information to a given query. The experiments below vary how the search tool is implemented: embedding only, embedding plus reranking, and with different models for each. The LLM powering the agent, tools, task set, corpus, and execution policy remain fixed while the retrieval configuration changes. We measure the agent's ability to find the relevant information for each task and total agent inference tokens per task, including input and output tokens across all turns.
*Figure 1. End-to-end task success versus total agent inference tokens per task across retrieval configurations.*
* **Lower agent inference cost:** Adding Nemotron 3.5 Rerank reduces agentic token cost per query by approximately 14% with Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B, and 13% with Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B, while improving retrieval accuracy in both configurations.
* **Better evidence within the same agent budget:** With Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B as the retriever, Nemotron 3.5 Rerank delivered approximately 0.9 points higher nDCG@10 than Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B at a similar agentic token cost.
## Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank
Behind these agent successes are Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Nemotron 3.5 Rerank, which retrieve evidence across text and images and prioritize it for the agent’s context. Nemotron 3.5 Embed builds on the previous generation’s Nemotron 3 Embed text embedding models to retrieve evidence from document images, including tables, charts, infographics, datasheets, and schematics. This allows applications to search information conveyed by visual content alongside document text.
The four models provide different options for retrieval and second-stage ranking:
|Model|Role|Deployment focus|
|Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B-BF16|Retrieves evidence across text and images, with strong multilingual retrieval capabilities.|Quality-focused search over text and visually rich documents|
|Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16|Distills the 8B model’s multimodal retrieval capabilities into a compact model.|Multimodal indexing and query serving with a smaller model footprint|
|Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-NVFP4|Applies NVFP4 quantization to both text and image encoders for efficient multimodal inference.|Large-scale document indexing and high-throughput retrieval on supported hardware|
|Nemotron-3.5-Rerank-8B-BF16|Jointly evaluates query–document pairs to refine relevance ranking across text and image candidates.|Selecting relevant evidence from retrieved candidates for RAG and agentic workflows|
*Table 1. Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Nemotron 3.5 Rerank model capabilities and use cases across various sizes and variants.*
Key features include:
* **Text and image retrieval:** Search document text and images containing tables, charts, infographics, datasheets, and schematics.
* **Multilingual support:** Text retrieval was evaluated across 34 languages, while multilingual visual retrieval was evaluated on MIRACL Vision (18 languages) and KoViDoRe. The model may support additional languages beyond those evaluated.
* **Multimodal reranking:** An 8B cross-encoder scores query–document pairs across text and image inputs.
* **BF16 and NVFP4 deployment:** The 1B embedding model is available in BF16 and NVFP4, with quantization applied to both text and image encoders.
* **Domain adaptation:**Nemotron embedding fine-tuning recipes support custom document collections, with a 18% and 3% relative nDCG@10 gain for Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16 and Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B-BF16 respectively in our chart and infographic experiments.
### Leading Multimodal Dense Retrieval on ViDoRe v3
On ViDoRe v3.1, Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B BF16 achieves 61.17 nDCG@10, ranking first among dense retrieval models. This is an 8.94-point improvement over the 52.23 score achieved by the Llama Nemotron Embed VL 1B model. The 1B model brings most of this visual retrieval quality into a smaller model. Distilled from the 8B teacher, Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B BF16 scores 58.38 nDCG@10, retaining 95.4% of the teacher’s score.
*Figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B BF16 ranked first among dense retrieval models on the ViDoRe v3.1 leaderboard as of 10/20/2026.*
We also compare the models with Qwen3-VL-Embedding, EmbeddingGemma-2, and the previous-generation NVIDIA model across ViDoRe v3, Korean ViDoRe and MIRACL Vision. The chart below reports retrieval accuracy for image-only and combined image-and-text inputs.
*Figure 3. Text and visual retrieval performance of Nemotron 3.5 Embed compared with prior-generation models and selected baselines.*
The multilingual results show how the models retrieve evidence across different language settings. On MIRACL Vision, the 8B model achieves 72.6 nDCG@10, exceeding Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 4.3 points. We also evaluate the models on KoViDoRe; both Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B and 1B outperform the Qwen baselines when using combined image and text inputs.
### Reranking the Evidence for Agent Tasks
Embedding models make large collections searchable by representing content as vectors. After retrieval returns a candidate set, Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B BF16 evaluates each candidate against the query to refine the ordering across text and image inputs. By distinguishing broadly related content from evidence that directly answers the question, the reranker helps agents use their context budget more effectively and focus on information needed to complete the task. For agentic retrieval systems, surfacing the strongest evidence earlier can reduce distracting context and help agents produce more grounded, efficient responses.
In collaboration with the MTEB team, we are launching the ViDoRe v3.1 reranking leaderboard to benchmark rerankers on document retrieval across image-only, text-only, and combined image-and-text inputs. Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B BF16 achieves 60.49 nDCG@10 with combined image-and-text inputs compared with Qwen-3-VL-Reranker-8B’s 59.17.
*Figure 4. Nemotron-3.5-Rerank-8B-BF16 ranked first on ViDoRe v3.1 Reranking leaderboard as of 10/20/2026.*
*Figure 5. Text and visual reranker performance of Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B compared with Qwen 3 VL Reranker 8B. Both models reranked the top 50 candidates retrieved by the Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B model.*
### Scaling Multimodal Retrieval with NVFP4
Retrieval quality is only part of the equation for production agentic systems. As document collections and query volumes grow, teams must balance accuracy, throughput, and infrastructure requirements.
Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B NVFP4 provides an optimized deployment option for high-throughput multimodal retrieval. On NVIDIA GB200, it delivers 27.1% higher throughput compared with the 1B BF16 model, increasing from 101.3 to 128.8 documents per second while retaining 99.85% of its retrieval accuracy on ViDoRe v3 with combined image and text inputs. As Figure 6 shows, the NVFP4 model offers a strong accuracy-throughput tradeoff for teams scaling retrieval across production workloads.
This deployment flexibility complements domain-specific customization: teams can select the data type of model weights that fits their infrastructure, then adapt the embedding and reranking models to their own terminology, documents, and retrieval tasks.
*Figure 6. ViDoRe V3 retrieval accuracy versus serving efficiency, comparing Nemotron 3.5 Embed with selected smaller open embedding baselines.*
### High-Performance Serving with NVIDIA NIM
NVIDIA NIM provides a high-performance deployment path for Nemotron 3.5 Embed. In testing on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, NIM delivered 6,031 query requests per second—approximately 2.9× the throughput of a comparable vLLM configuration at 2,099 requests per second—while maintaining comparable passage-processing throughput. This optimized serving stack helps enterprises scale retrieval workloads with production-ready deployment and support.
*Figure 7. Nemotron 3.5 Embed NIM serving performance compared with the vLLM checkpoint on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs.*
### Adapting Retrieval to Domain-Specific Tasks
Enterprise agents often search documents containing specialized terminology and company-specific information that general-purpose retrieval models may not fully capture. Fine-tuning allows teams to adapt Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank using their own documents, queries, and relevance labels to their specific domains and use cases.
The Nemotron multimodal embedding fine-tuning recipe combines synthetic data generation, hard-negative mining, fine-tuning with NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel, and evaluation in one workflow. Teams can generate queries and relevance labels from their own documents to build training data for their retrieval tasks.
We evaluated the recipe on 8,202 chart and infographic images using 8,591 synthetic queries generated with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, focusing on enumerative and open-ended queries with multiple relevant images. Fine-tuning the Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16 on 6,872 queries for one epoch increased nDCG@10 from 37.34 to 44.12, a 18% relative gain over the base model, on 1,719 held-out synthetic queries. Using the same synthetic queries set, fine-tuning Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B-BF16 for epoch increased nDCG@10 from 41.44 to 42.75, a 3% relative gain.
### How We Built the Embed and Rerank Models
Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B builds on Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, with its language component initialized from Nemotron-3-Embed-8B-BF16. The model is trained on image and text corpora using contrastive learning to produce representations for multimodal retrieval.
The Embed 1B models are distilled from Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B, with their language component initialized from Nemotron-3-Embed-1B-BF16. Distillation combines cosine and mean squared error (MSE) losses to align the student’s embeddings with the teacher’s.
The language component remains frozen throughout embedding-model training. Text-only embeddings are therefore expected to remain unchanged from the corresponding Nemotron 3 Embed models, allowing existing text embeddings and vector indexes to be reused.
Nemotron 3.5 Rerank uses the same backbone architecture as Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B in a cross-encoder configuration. While the embedding model encodes queries and documents separately and scores their similarity, the reranker jointly encodes each query–document pair. A final multilayer perceptron (MLP) scoring head produces a scalar relevance logit.
All models are trained on a mixture of publicly available and synthetic multilingual, multimodal data, and their final released weights are produced through checkpoint ensembling. Further details on the training data are available in each model’s Hugging Face model card.
## Nemotron 3.5 Parse
Enterprise knowledge often arrives in PDFs whose embedded text captures only part of what is on the page. Extracting that text can lose reading order, separate table values from their headers, or omit information conveyed in charts. Scanned documents and image-based PDFs may contain no usable text layer at all. Before this information can support search, retrieval, or automated document workflows, the pixels need to become structured content.
Nemotron 3.5 Parse converts document images into machine-readable text while preserving the structure that gives the content meaning. It identifies document elements, their locations, and reading order, and extracts tables and charts into structured representations. The resulting Markdown, HTML tables, and structured blocks give developers content that is better suited to indexing, search, and downstream processing. Applications can retrieve a passage with its surrounding context, process a table as rows and columns, and link extracted evidence back to its location on the original page.
At 631 million parameters, Nemotron 3.5 Parse brings this capability to document pipelines at scale, complementing Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank with structured information for retrieval and agent workflows.
### Leading Accuracy with Faster Document Processing
*Figure 8. Nemotron 3.5 Parse ranked first on ParseBench leaderboard among models with fewer than 1 billion parameters as of 10/20/2026.*
Nemotron 3.5 Parse ranks #1 on ParseBench among models with fewer than 1 billion parameters, achieving a score of 75.20 while processing 10.5 pages per second on one NVIDIA H100. It delivers best-in-class speed with well optimized parameter allocation, multi-token prediction, speculative decoding and flexible native-resolution handling. ParseBench tests table and chart extraction, content faithfulness, semantic formatting, and visual grounding.
Developers can scale processing toward speed or accuracy using the same model. Single-pass inference extracts each page once for the highest throughput. Double-pass inference revisits tables and charts identified in the initial page parse. Triple-pass inference adds a detection pass to find additional regions for refinement. This approach concentrates additional processing on document regions that benefit from a closer look.
|Processing mode|ParseBench score ↑|Pages per second on one H100 ↑|
|Single pass|72.74|16.1|
|Double pass|74.92|11.2|
|Triple pass|75.20|10.5|
*Table 2. Model accuracy is able to scale with additional model passes at a small cost to throughput. Reprocessing focused crops of tables and charts leads to increased accuracy.*
All three configurations are Pareto optimal within this comparison: no other compared configuration achieves both higher accuracy and higher throughput. Teams can choose the operating point that fits their workload, from rapid ingestion of large document collections to more detailed extraction of complex pages.
*Figure 9. Nemotron Parse 3.5 achieves pareto optimal performance on ParseBench leaderboard.*
### How We Built Nemotron 3.5 Parse
Nemotron 3.5 Parse is trained on a diverse mixture of enterprise documents, scientific papers, forms, tables, charts, and multilingual text. A strong synthetic data engine expands the range of layouts, structures, and languages the model sees, complementing automatically labeled documents and human-labeled data. This diversity prepares the model for the varied content found in enterprise document collections. Model card and multilingual coverage.
We further improve robustness and reliability through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using custom reward functions to reinforce correct document structure and penalize failures. This post-training reduces repetitive generation loops and unclosed blocks, improves table consistency, and strengthens adherence to chart schemas, making extracted information more reliable for downstream document workflows.

signals.title: Specter MoE System Reports 1.88x Peak Single-GPU Speedup | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
# Specter MoE System Reports 1.88x Peak Single-GPU Speedup 

 By Alexis Dufresne · Published October 21, 2026 at 08:09 UTC · Updated October 21, 2026 at 08:30 UTC 

## TL;DR

- Specter reports an average 1.50x speedup in time per output token, peaking at 1.88x, against the state-of-the-art MoE inference system on single-GPU hardware.
- A quantized draft model runs on the GPU while experts live in host memory; multi-step routing lookahead lets the runtime pre-stage expert transfers over PCIe.
- The authors have released code and the measured gains cover single-request inference only, not batched or multi-tenant serving.

Specter, a new MoE inference system, reports an average 1.50x speedup in time per output token with peaks hitting 1.88x over the state-of-the-art on commodity single-GPU hardware, according to its authors on Hugging Face. The paper targets a familiar bottleneck. Mixture-of-experts models often exceed a single accelerator's memory, so experts get pushed out to host memory, and the resulting PCIe traffic sits on the critical path because routing is data-dependent.

The method pairs quantization with speculative decoding. "Its lightweight quantized draft model runs efficiently on device while preserving high-fidelity expert activation patterns," the authors write, which gives the runtime "accurate multi-step lookahead over future expert usage" so expert movement can be organized ahead of verification rather than reactively.

Code is posted at the paper's GitHub repository. The reported speedups cover single-request inference; the abstract does not break out batched-throughput or multi-tenant numbers. The result arrives in a busy week for MoE-inference work on our tracker, alongside Lafa's flow language model earlier the same day.

# Introducing vLLM TorchTPU

October 20, 2026 6 min read

Table of Contents

Today we're releasing vLLM TorchTPU (`vllm-torchtpu`), a new backend for running vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It's built on Google's TorchTPU stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code.

This work comes out of the engineering partnership between Inferact and Google we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to:

1. Make it easy to bring new models to TPU by reusing vLLM's existing model code.
2. Push TPU inference performance in open source, with Pallas kernels for attention, Mixture-of-Experts, and quantized matmul.
3. Keep the vLLM experience the same: the same CLI, OpenAI-compatible server, scheduler, and KV cache manager you use on other hardware.

...

### How It Works

`vllm-torchtpu` is an out-of-tree vLLM platform plugin. Once installed, vLLM picks it up automatically through the `vllm.platform_plugins` entry point.

Models run through vLLM's standard model runner and are compiled with `torch.compile(backend="tpu")`, which lowers to XLA. Each TPU device gets its own worker process, the same way vLLM runs on GPUs, and communication between devices goes through `torch.distributed`. This means the scheduler,

...

### Models, Features, and What's Next

`vllm-torchtpu` can serve most models supported by vLLM, with TPU-specific kernel, quantization, and parallelism work for the Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Llama, GPT-OSS, and Gemma families. TPU v7x (Ironwood) is the recommended hardware and is tested in CI on every pull request; v6e, v5e, and v5p are experimental.

The Supported Models & Features page has the full list of validated checkpoints and features, with how to enable each one. The nightly support matrices track TPU v7x correctness and benchmark results from CI.

...

#### What's Next?

We want new open models from the major families (Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, Gemma, GPT-OSS) to run on TPU on the day they're released. Some of what's coming, from the public roadmap:

- An automated CI pipeline that onboards, benchmarks, and publishes support matrices for new open-weight models within 24 hours of release.
- Prefix-, cache-, and session-aware routing, and llm-d TPU memory-tier routing.
- PyTorch interfaces for Tokamax kernels, shared with other projects in the TorchTPU ecosystem.
- Diffusion model serving through `vllm-omni`.

Contributions are welcome!

signals.excerpt:
EAGLE 4 on AMD Instinct GPUs

# EAGLE-4 on AMD Instinct GPUs from day 0

 Oct 20, 2026

EAGLE-4, the newest drafter from the EAGLE team, runs on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs from day 0, in SGLang and ATOM. - On Qwen3.8-27B, one MI355X GPU serves a single request at ~300 tokens/s in BF16: 3.5x plain decoding and 1.6x the model’s built-in MTP. - The gain holds as load grows, from 1 to 32 concurrent conversations, and scales to four GPUs. It works out of the box: the same checkpoint and the same serving flags as on other hardware.

...

## What is new in EAGLE-4

Speculative decoding lets a small drafter guess several tokens ahead, and the large model checks them all in one pass. EAGLE-4 adds three ideas on top of the EAGLE family:

- One drafter for every batch size and every GPU. EAGLE-4 drafts one token at a time, so it can stop, deepen or widen its guess tree at every step. EAGLE-Harness measures what drafting and verifying cost on the actual hardware, once at start-up. During serving it picks the tree that gives the most accepted tokens per unit of cost: a wide, deep tree for a single user, short chains under heavy load.
- A cheaper LM head for the drafter. The drafter’s vocabulary projection used to be most of its cost. A low-rank head first shortlists candidates from the full vocabulary, then the full head scores only those exactly. This cuts the draft’s cost by more than 40% without truncating the vocabulary.
- A small drafter. One transformer layer, so it fits next to the model with little memory, from data-center GPUs down to edge devices.

...

## Day 0 on AMD Instinct GPUs

EAGLE-4 runs on the MI355X GPU with the same checkpoint and the same launch flags as elsewhere:

To make it fast on day 0, we measured EAGLE-Harness’s cost tables on the MI355X GPU, so tree sizes fit this GPU; added tree verification for Qwen3.8’s linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) layers: a guess tree is checked in one pass, and only the accepted branch’s state is kept; checked losslessness: every output token matches plain decoding, up to BF16 rounding at near-ties.

#### llm-d for distributed LLM inference

To run inference engines across large fleets, we are releasing llm-d 1.0 with Red Hat, IBM, and a community of more than 500 contributors and 25 organizations. llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale

# llm-d 1.0 Advances Open, Cost-Efficient AI Inference for Production Scale

- llm-d 1.0 consolidates a hardened core for distributed inference validated for day 2 production deployments that helps organizations improve AI serving efficiency and scale enterprise workloads.
- llm-d is broadly adopted and trusted by frontier model labs, hyperscalers and neoclouds, hardware accelerators, and major enterprises, with recent demonstrations showing up to five to 10 times cost reductions for context-heavy agentic workloads 1 and three times greater output throughput. 2 

SAN JOSE, C.A. - October 20, 2026 —

Today, llm-d project contributors announced the release of llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for the open source project designed to help organizations deploy and scale large language model inference more efficiently across modern infrastructure. Founded in 2025 by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), llm-d plays a key role in the open foundation for enterprises deploying AI at scale in production.

...

With the rise of agentic AI, new types of workloads are placing a different kind of stress on infrastructure systems. Agentic workloads continually access and reuse vast amounts of context while supporting parallel agents that can generate unpredictable bursts of activity. Managing that context often consumes more resources than generating the final output itself, making latency, throughput, memory efficiency and infrastructure costs critical factors in realizing AI return on investment. llm-d already delivers hardware heterogeneity and advanced inference capabilities out of the box for complex infrastructure environments, as well as prefix-cache and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch and async inference—across multiple model servers, including vLLM and SGLang.

...

llm-d 1.0 is engineered to bring that performance to the realities of Day 2 operations and the ongoing work of running inference in production: serving multiple tenants, balancing competing priorities, providing with zero downtime features and supporting emerging agentic workloads, all within one suite of co-designed components that compose into a platform. New capabilities in 1.0 include:

- Multi-tenant quality of service — Priority and fairness-aware flow control helps latency-sensitive requests, and bursty agent workloads share a fleet without starving one another.
- Zero-downtime operations — Router high availability with hot standby and rolling updates keep traffic flowing through upgrades and planned maintenance. Management of prefill/decode replicas as one logical unit, with coordinated rollouts and lockstep upgrades—making disaggregated serving practical in production.
- A stable foundation to build on — A v1 configuration API and a hardened request path, validated across clouds and accelerators, give adopters a release they can standardize on.
- Agent-aware serving — Session-aware routing keeps multi-turn conversations close to their cached context, while turn-priority scheduling and native Responses API state support help agents reuse context across turns and reduce recomputation.

...

In one recent use case, open frontier models and llm-d enabled IBM Research to explore quantum error correction hardware at 11.5 times lower inference cost than an all-proprietary configuration. Researchers reported a prefix-cache hit rate of approximately 98% and a blended serving cost of about $0.11 per million tokens.

In a separate recent demonstration using benchmark workloads, researchers showed that llm-d could efficiently serve large mixture-of-experts models for agentic workloads. Researchers used llm-d to deploy GLM 5.2, an approximately 753-billion-parameter open-weight model, on widely deployed NVIDIA GPUs, demonstrating how enterprises can use existing GPU fleets to serve frontier-class AI at scale. On a workload with hundreds of agentic sessions running in parallel, the deployment delivered over 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak on agentic benchmarks, serving up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents with zero preemptions. At current cloud rental rates, this deployment led to costs that would have been 5 to 10 times less per token than equivalent commercial API pricing, with the largest savings on the input-heavy traffic patterns typical of agentic workloads, highlighting how llm-d can save resources and costs for enterprises deploying AI in production at scale.

signals.title: RuVector: Self-Learning Vector Database for AI Agent Memory
signals.excerpt:
What RuVector Does

- Search and relationships in one engine. Fast vector search (HNSW indexing with SIMD acceleration, sub-millisecond queries) works alongside a Cypher-compatible knowledge graph. An agent can find similar material and follow how facts relate without a second database.
- Improves retrieval from explicitly recorded feedback. When teams record which results helped, SONA updates lightweight LoRA adapters, and EWC++ consolidation protects earlier learning. Reads alone never change learned weights. Adapter learning is separate from index tuning and ranking settings, which teams control directly.
- Works inside PostgreSQL. The ruvector-postgres extension is pgvector-compatible and adds 143 SQL functions for vector, graph and hybrid search inside an existing database. Teams should confirm compatibility for their specific pgvector workloads; full migration details are in the technical guide.
- Signed, portable memory. The RVF file format packages vectors, indexes and metadata in a single file with copy-on-write branching and SHAKE256 witness chains, a tamper-evident record of every change. The same memory runs on servers, in WebAssembly in the browser and on edge devices, and running locally avoids hosted vector-service fees.

candidates.angle: Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 provides compact, open-weight, multimodal embeddings (text, code, images, video, audio) optimized for efficient RAG and semantic search.
candidates.audience_pain: Building RAG systems for diverse data types beyond text is complex, requiring specialized multimodal embedding solutions.
candidates.why_now: EmbeddingGemma 2, released under Apache 2.0, is a new open-weight model expanding multimodal capabilities for RAG.

candidates.angle: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed, Rerank, and Parse models significantly improve AI agent performance by ensuring more relevant evidence retrieval, reducing wasted tokens.
candidates.audience_pain: AI agents often struggle with irrelevant or incomplete information retrieval, leading to poor performance and higher token costs.
candidates.why_now: NVIDIA's new Nemotron 3.5 series directly addresses a critical pain point for advancing agents, improving grounding and efficiency.
candidates.hook_seed: Better agent retrieval, less token waste.

candidates.topic: Meta's Muse Spark Open for Agent Work
candidates.angle: Meta's Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1M-token context window, is optimized for long-horizon coding and agent work, surpassing proprietary models in benchmarks.
candidates.audience_pain: Developers need powerful, open-weight models with extensive context for complex agentic tasks and long coding sessions.
candidates.why_now: Muse Spark Open, a leading open-weight MoE model, was just released, offering capabilities that rival or exceed proprietary models for agentic applications.
candidates.hook_seed: Meta's new open MoE for agents.

candidates.angle: DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, the inference framework behind its production services, addressing the 'core problem' of serving large models cost-effectively at scale.
candidates.audience_pain: Building and operating an inference framework capable of serving massive user bases efficiently and affordably is a significant engineering challenge.
candidates.why_now: DeepSeek, a major AI startup, just open-sourced its battle-tested production inference framework, offering valuable insights and tools to the community.
candidates.hook_seed: DeepSeek opens its LLM inference engine.

candidates.topic: Humming: Fast Kernels for Quantized Inference
candidates.angle: Humming offers a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference, boosting efficiency across diverse hardware (NVIDIA, T-Head) and quantization schemes.
candidates.audience_pain: Optimizing quantized LLM inference for performance and broad hardware compatibility often requires custom kernel development.
candidates.why_now: Ant Group and the vLLM community open-sourced Humming, a new library specifically designed for fast, flexible quantized inference.
candidates.hook_seed: Faster quantized LLM inference, open source.

candidates.topic: vLLM TorchTPU: Run vLLM on TPUs
candidates.angle: vLLM TorchTPU enables running vLLM models on Google Cloud TPUs with existing model code and the same CLI, expanding hardware options for high-performance inference.
candidates.audience_pain: Developers want to leverage TPUs for cost-efficient, high-performance LLM inference, but native support for popular frameworks like vLLM was lacking.
candidates.why_now: TorchTPU is now open source, and vLLM released a native backend for running on Google Cloud TPUs, making these powerful accelerators more accessible.
candidates.hook_seed: Run vLLM models on TPUs. Now.

candidates.angle: EAGLE-4 enhances speculative decoding on AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, achieving up to 3.5x speedup for LLM inference (e.g., Qwen3.8-27B) from day zero, offering a strong alternative to NVIDIA.
candidates.audience_pain: Achieving high-performance, cost-effective LLM inference, especially on alternative hardware like AMD GPUs, is a constant challenge for developers.
candidates.why_now: EAGLE-4's day-zero support for AMD MI355X GPUs, with significant speedups, provides a compelling new option for inference acceleration.

candidates.topic: Neo4j Context Engine for AI Agents
candidates.angle: The Neo4j Context Engine provides a knowledge layer for enterprise AI agents, using GraphRAG retrievers to pull context from a semantic layer for improved grounding.
candidates.audience_pain: Enterprise AI agents often lack robust, real-time access to company-specific knowledge, leading to ungrounded or inaccurate responses.
candidates.why_now: Neo4j is addressing a critical need for enterprise agents with its new Context Engine, leveraging knowledge graphs for better context management.
